talks.title: Food and Drug Administration: Medical Device Cybersecurity Ethics
talks.teaser: FDA Cyber Policy Advisor Jessica Wilkerson examines regulatory frameworks, vulnerability disclosure, and patient safety ethics in medical devices.
talks.summary:
In this keynote from the DEF CON Safe Mode Ethics Village, Jessica Wilkerson from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines the ethical, regulatory, and technical dimensions of medical device cybersecurity. Opening at 00:04, Jessica outlines the FDA's regulatory authority over medical devices and discusses inter-agency coordination with HHS and CISA.

At 04:00 and 08:00, she explores the delicate balance between patient safety and vulnerability research, highlighting coordinated vulnerability disclosure policies and public-private partnerships across the healthcare ecosystem.

Concluding at 12:00 and 16:01, Jessica analyzes the regulatory framework governing medical device recalls and software patching, praising pioneering researchers and device manufacturers who embraced ethical vulnerability disclosure to protect patient well-being. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: TechCongress: Bridging Technologists and Congressional Policy
talks.teaser: Leisel Bogan discusses TechCongress fellows embedding technical expertise into congressional committees to shape technology legislation.
talks.summary:
Andrea Matwyshyn hosts TechCongress senior congressional fellow Leisel Bogan in the Ethics Village to examine how technical experts directly influence national legislation and digital policy on Capitol Hill [00:03, 00:09].

Bogan shares insights from her fellowship working inside congressional committees, focusing on cyber-enabled disinformation campaigns, troll farms, and deepfake proliferation [09:05, 18:22]. She explains the critical knowledge gap between lawmakers and technologists, illustrating how technical fellows help draft precise legislative language that avoids unintended consequences for security researchers [27:46, 36:31]. Bogan urges security researchers, engineers, and digital rights advocates to participate in civil service fellowships to bridge the gap between technical reality and federal lawmaking [45:37].
